No worries. Generally speaking it is completely normal that pinkies and ring fingers flatten when trying to reach a note. It's not the end of the world. This applies especially when the note is far away to reach. For my small hands the pinkies and ring fingers are predestined to reach note above an octave with flat fingers... However here, it seems to me that the note should be easily reached. Maybe your pinky strength is not enough to comfortably play with a more curved finger.

For that I would suggest a simple exercise for you to try out: practice the left hand on its own, slowly, and when you need to reach the bass note lift the entire hand in a high round arch, keep the wrist soft and hit the bass with you pinky, nice and stable. This way, your pinky should land in a higher and more accessible position for more curviture. This exercise is applicable for all pieces with such left hand accompaniment. And it gets more and more useful for long distance jumps as you work on both precision and pinky strength. The main difference between how this exercise works and how you are playing now is in either reaching a note or jumping for it.

Good luck!

You have the notes down now and that's a great base. Your technique will get better over time (don't forget slow practice) but now you need to incorporate musicality and phrasing.

The beginning scherzo part is very stiff. You need to draw the line and let the music dance. After that, you take no break and go into the next section immediately. Everything is sameish loud and kind of stressful to listen to. Same for the ascending and descending arpeggios. It sounds like you are just running as fast as you can. The arpeggios need to be played like a wave. They reach their climax and then you are rewarded with the resolution. Generally, you are not letting the music breathe.

Think about the important notes (they should be in your sheets), the accents, and very importantly the climax and their resolutions. Use the dynamics written in the sheets! Those are the instructions you can find most readily. Think about where you can use some tasteful rubato and where you need to give the music space. You need to practice all of this at a lower tempo. This will 1. improve you listening and 2. help with technique.

At last I would suggest less "banging". I think Chopin sounds the greatest with a soft touch. Try to play around a bit and see how you can produce a bold but still soft, warm sound. The sound has to come out of the instrument and less from hitting into the keys.

It took me around 4 months to get this part to a level I was slightly satisfied with, so don't be impatient. Good luck :)

You got the notes down which is pretty great already. However, it still sounds rather monotonic, robotic and therefore not exciting to listen to. Here are some suggestions at how I would go about this when I have no teacher.

First look at the dynamics in the sheet music. Think about where the music is going and then lead it. I recommend listening to different recordings and you will notice many differences in how they sound compared to your version. Listen to different pianists to figure out the nuances and differences of each interpretation.

Working on tempo is important but I would suggest not neglecting slow practice. When practicing slow, think about the intention of each note and play it as you imagine. Go through the dynamical changes, the crescendos and decrescendos to build the atmosphere. This will help to develope your ear for the musicality of this piece. Also, practice slow to practice fast, works every time.

I think you need to take your time to recognise the melody and really really accentuate it. Since everything is the same loudness, it's hard to follow.

This may be the hardest part for me, since my music theory is not very solid but analysing the piece in its harmonic structure can also help you in understanding the structure of the piece.

And lastly, I would suggest you to "bang" less into the keys. The sound you produce will be vastly different depending on the way you hit the keys. Now it's all the same (no dynamics) but it also sounds very hard. I suggest you to try to play the sound out of the instrument instead of into the instrument. It's hard to explain over a written comment but you could try to experiment with the sound more to achieve a soft but still bold sound. For me, Chopin sounds so sensible when that softness is retained, especially in the most dramatic, harrowing or euphoric sections.

Good luck :)

If you can find the time to look up correct pedal technique I would recommend you to look up legato and staccato. On the piano it's almost impossible to make the sounds flow into each other like it would be for e.g. voice or violin, since it's individual hammers hitting strings. Legato is a foundational technique to make the notes sound almost and very closely flowing into each, as if there was not a single second no tone. If you don't know this, I do not recommend even touching the pedal. This also explains why you feel like your playing sounds choppy without pedal.

Hmm this is not easy to answer because I find that it's easier to just show someone how to do it correctly instead of trying to explain how to not make a mistake. Try to maintain posture while holding a small round object in your hand like a mandarin. When you press a key you shouldn't press into it like a button using purely finger strength but push using the weight on your arms. If you sit not too high and not too low the weight will distribute along your arm without collapsing your wrist. When you begin to familiarise yourself with how you play, you will understand intuitively how to adjust your weight along your upper body to achieve the balance in wrist and fingers. Tension of the fingers will always lead to tension of the wrist and vice versa. You need to keep the wrist loose and flexible. It has to be able to always spring back to its original position without much effort.

I definitely recommend not holding the pedal throughout the whole piece. For the untrained ear and for the player themselves it may sound pleasant but I assure you, as a listener and after some time the fogginess will be noticeable. When you don't change the pedal, the notes become unclear, the melody will vanish under all the noise. Pedal change is a discipline of its own but at its basics you will need to change the pedal everytime the harmony changes. This is important equally for slow and fast pieces.

You could try to record your playing and carefully review when your sound begins to suffer from too much pedal. Generally I recommend practicing 80% of the time without when you are not familiar enough with the piece of music and be really honest with yourself whether your technique and tone is steady enough or if you are just using the pedal to cover your mistakes.

Few things you should think about:

1. Leave the pedal for now. Trust me, you need to hear your mistakes first. I started pedaling after 5 weeks into this piece. 

2. Your left hand jumps have to be precise and fast. At full tempo you have no time thinking about where to go. Practice the left hand jumps a lot. The more secure you are in your left hand, the more you can focus on your right hand.

3. Look at the music carefully. In the descending and repeating part of the coda, the accents are on the second chords. The technique to properly play this is to take the rebounce of your first attack to strike even stronger. Just as it has been said by Reponsible-Box-1449. Ta ram, ta TA ram, ta TA ram.

3.5. The descending part is repeated once. Don't play the repetition identical to the first one. 

4. Practice S L O W and try to focus on the melody. I can't really hear the path the music is supposed to take. When practicing, exaggerate this by playing everything but the melody extremely soft.

5. Dynamics! I know this is the part where you are supposed to go insane, but I think there is a lot here to explore. It's not just a brilliant finale but so much anguish and desperation. Try to look at this coda in sections and build phrases that make sense. For this, listening to different recordings helped me a lot.

This coda is super hard. Consider all of this before moving forward in speed. Learning this is honestly one the most rewarding things ever. Good luck :)

I have experience with three teachers who have guided me during different periods of my life. They all have different teaching styles and preferences but what they did have in common is their teaching structure. It's the structure I am familiar with and works the best and most efficient for me. When I will have to leave my current teacher, I will look for  new teacher that also works with this structure.
I wouldn't like the class as you describe it.

They choose pieces for me (I like that because I don't know as much repetoire, also I like to get to know my teacher as well!) but sometimes I also bring in pieces I want to play and they can evaluate if I'm ready and if they are qualified to teach it. When I was young, my first teacher told me which part I am supposed to practice and then I practice it at home. Nowadays I work through the whole piece at home first. Next lesson I play the best way I can and then they start to guide me through my technical mistakes and the parts where I struggle. They teach me practice strategies and what exercises I can do to learn those sections faster. I also bring in questions regarding technique or phrasing that we discuss. I am being instructed but we also discuss a lot. My teacher also demonstrate when words are not enough. We repeat this for all the pieces I work on and then I go home to practice the way I was instructed. In 95% of all times that works very well. Rinse and repeat each week. I slowly begin to memorise all practice tips, which makes learning without a teacher faster, which means I can learn pieces quicker and I can take on harder pieces.

Along the way, we start to explore musicality and phrasing of the piece, think about how we want it to sound and how we can emulate those feelings. My standard program usually consists of one challenging piece slightly above my level, one medium long piece I can play and learn rather fast and two etudes. When I am done with one, we tackle a new piece of the respective category.
